title: Heard, not written
hookLine: say it after me: a song passed from one mouth to another, no page in sight. Tradition says the Rig Veda was heard, then carried by voice
carry: the vedas are shruti: heard, and handed on by voice

cards: A grandmother sits on the edge of a bed and sings one line of an old song. The child sings it back, a little off. She sings it again, slower.
The child tries again, and this time it lands. Next line. Nobody opens a book.
The song moves from one mouth into one ear, and lives there now. Years later that child might sing it to someone else, the same way, line by line.
Hindu tradition says the Rig Veda traveled this way, and it has a name for it.

teach.b: The Vedas are called shruti, what is heard. Tradition says the hymns weren't invented the way a song is written today.

teach.h: SEEN BY RISHIS, PASSED BY MOUTH.
teach.b: They were seen and heard by rishis, seers, in a kind of deep listening, then passed on by mouth, teacher to student.
Tradition remembers each hymn with its seer, its god and its meter, so a chanter knows whose hymn it is and how it should sound.

Some schools of interpretation, Mimamsa among them, go further: the Veda has no human author at all. The seers didn't make it; they received it. And yet the hymns sometimes speak of themselves another way.
In one hymn to Agni the poet says, in paraphrase: I have fashioned this praise for you, as a skilled maker builds a chariot. Fitted, shaped, joined.

So the tradition holds two pictures side by side: the hymn is heard, and the hymn is crafted with care. Some teachers hold them together: a seer can receive something and still work hard to say it well.
That's why the sound matters so much. Vedic chanters learn the words not only straight through but in patterns that repeat and weave them, so a slip would be caught.

teach.h: THE SOUND IS PART OF THE GIFT.
teach.b: The meaning matters, but in this tradition the sound itself is part of what's handed on. That's why a pandit at a havan may stop you over a single syllable: you've joined a long chain of voices.

how: Vedic recitation is traditionally learned by ear from a teacher, the student repeating each phrase back, and chanters also learn recitation patterns that repeat and interweave the words to keep the sound exact.

games.q: what does “what the rig veda is” mean?
o: hymns heard by seers and carried by voice
poems one king wrote down for his court
a book of rules first carved on stone

games.q: how the hymns are carried — tap the pairs.
p: a seer who saw and heard the hymns
the Veda has no human author

s: the Vedas are called shruti: tradition says they were heard by seers and carried by voice.
the hymns never speak of poets shaping them
one poet says he fashioned his praise for Agni as a skilled maker builds a chariot.
in this tradition, only the meaning matters, not the sound
chanters learn the words in patterns that repeat and weave them, so the sound is kept exact.

games.q: you're a student of Vedic chant. your teacher has just chanted a line. what do you do next?
o: write it down so you won't forget.
say it back, sound for sound.
ask what it means before going on.
games.why: tradition teaches by ear: the student repeats the line back, sound for sound, and the meaning is studied too.

practice: Close your eyes and listen to the room, the near sounds first, then the far ones, receiving them without naming or judging, the way a seer is said to receive a hymn.

If a prayer or chant someone taught you by heart comes to mind, a shloka or a line of a bhajan, let it play quietly and notice whose voice it's in; if you pray, you can thank the people who carried words to you.

wordCard.voice: What the Rig Veda is. Shruti, what is heard: hymns tradition says were seen by rishis and carried by voice, while one poet calls his hymn something fashioned like a chariot.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a seer. Tradition says the rishis saw and heard the Vedic hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: the vedas are shruti: heard, and handed on by voice. Heard by seers, crafted like a chariot, and carried mouth to ear. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 5.2.11 (this praise I have fashioned for you, Agni, as a skilled maker a chariot)
shruti, the rishis as seers, and the Mimamsa view of the Veda as authorless (apaurusheya)
